steps.tx: While the Bohr effect describes how carbon dioxide and acidity alter oxygen binding, reciprocal regulation of carbon dioxide transport by oxygenation is designated the **Haldane effect**. Specifically, deoxygenation of blood increases its capacity to carry carbon dioxide, whereas oxygenation in the lungs promotes rapid carbon dioxide unloading.
steps.say: The Haldane effect describes how deoxygenated blood carries more carbon dioxide, whereas oxygenation promotes carbon dioxide release.

left.title: Bohr Effect (Oxygen Affinity)
points: Describes effect of PCO2 and pH on Hb-O2 affinity
Increased CO2 and H+ promote O2 unloading
Operates primarily at systemic tissue capillaries
Stabilizes deoxygenated T-state conformation

right.title: Haldane Effect (CO2 Carriage)
points: Describes effect of PO2 on Hb-CO2 carrying capacity
Deoxygenation promotes CO2 uptake and proton buffering
Operates reciprocally at tissue and alveolar capillaries
Accounts for ~50% of total CO2 exchange in blood

steps.tx: At the molecular level, deoxygenated haemoglobin is a significantly weaker acid and superior buffer compared to oxyhaemoglobin. When haemoglobin releases oxygen in peripheral tissues, the resulting deoxygenated conformation readily absorbs protons released by carbonic acid dissociation, buffering tissue acidity and driving **carbon dioxide uptake**.
steps.say: Deoxyhaemoglobin buffers hydrogen ions released during carbonic acid formation, pulling more carbon dioxide into venous blood.

nodes.label: Peripheral Capillaries: Oxyhaemoglobin (HbO2) Releases Oxygen into Tissues
Deoxy-Hb Formed: Becomes a Weaker Acid with Higher pKa
Deoxy-Hb Binds Free H+ Ions Generated from Carbonic Acid Dissociation
Equilibrium Pulls CO2 Inward: Venous Blood Carries Extra CO2 Without Acidosis

steps.tx: Furthermore, deoxygenated globin amine termini bind carbon dioxide directly with three times greater affinity than oxyhaemoglobin, forming **carbaminohaemoglobin complexes**. In peripheral capillaries, this affinity allows venous blood to transport substantial quantities of metabolic carbon dioxide with minimal change in venous carbon dioxide partial pressure.
steps.say: Deoxygenated globin binds carbon dioxide directly to form carbamino complexes with threefold higher affinity than oxyhaemoglobin.

left.title: Peripheral Tissue Capillaries
points: Low PO2 favours deoxyhaemoglobin formation
Enhanced binding of H+ ions buffers carbonic acid
Carbamino binding capacity triples
Haldane effect accounts for ~50% of CO2 exchange

right.title: Pulmonary Capillaries
points: High PO2 converts deoxyhaemoglobin to oxyhaemoglobin
Protons released from globin displace CO2 from bicarbonate
Carbamino groups rapidly dissociate
CO2 is released into alveoli and exhaled

steps.tx: Oxygen given carelessly to a chronic carbon dioxide retainer can deepen the problem it treats. **Worsening hypercapnia** follows high flow oxygen through reduced hypoxic drive, the Haldane effect releasing carbon dioxide from haemoglobin, and worsened ventilation perfusion matching in diseased lung. Controlled oxygen targeting lower saturations is therefore a prescription with a ceiling, not a reflex. A repeat gas after starting oxygen is how the harm is caught early.
steps.say: High flow oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in chronic retainers by several mechanisms. Controlled targets and a repeat gas catch the harm early.

steps.tx: The clinical relevance of the Haldane effect is starkly illustrated during oxygen therapy in severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Administering high-flow oxygen displaces carbon dioxide from haemoglobin into plasma before ventilation can eliminate it, precipitating acute **worsening hypercapnia** alongside loss of hypoxic ventilatory drive.
steps.say: Administering high-flow oxygen in severe COPD can acutely elevate blood carbon dioxide by displacing it from haemoglobin.

vis.caption: Carbon dioxide retention mechanisms and controlled oxygen therapy in advanced obstructive disease.

steps.tx: Intracellular regulation of oxygen unloading in red blood cells is controlled by **2,3-bisphosphoglycerate**, synthesized via the Rapoport-Luebering glycolytic shunt. A single molecule of this highly negatively charged polyanion binds within the positively charged central cavity between the two beta-globin chains of deoxygenated haemoglobin.
steps.say: Two, three-bisphosphoglycerate binds the central cavity between beta chains, stabilizing the deoxygenated state and releasing oxygen.

nodes.label: Bypass via BPG Mutase: Produces 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (Rapoport-Luebering Shunt)
Binds Positively Charged Lysine and Histidine in Beta-Globin Central Cavity
Cross-Links Beta Chains: Stabilizes Deoxy T-State and Raises P50

steps.tx: Stored red cells show **2,3-bisphosphoglycerate depletion** within one to two weeks, and the oxygen dissociation curve shifts left. Haemoglobin grips oxygen tightly, so transfused blood unloads poorly at the tissues until the Rapoport-Luebering shunt rebuilds the polyanion over a day. One molecule sits in the central cavity between the two beta chains of deoxyhaemoglobin and stabilises the low-affinity state. Without binding, tissue oxygen delivery falls when arterial saturation is preserved.

steps.tx: By stabilizing the tense deoxygenated conformation through ionic cross-links, 2,3-BPG reduces oxygen affinity and increases P50. Chronic exposure to hypobaric hypoxia at high altitude or severe chronic anaemia triggers adaptive increases in **erythrocyte 2,3-BPG synthesis**, shifting the dissociation curve rightward to maintain tissue delivery.
steps.say: Chronic hypoxia and anaemia stimulate 2,3-BPG synthesis, shifting the curve rightward to improve tissue oxygen delivery.

rows: Compensates for reduced total Hb concentration
Impaired oxygen release to tissues on transfusion

steps.tx: During prolonged storage in citrate-phosphate-dextrose anticoagulants, red blood cells experience progressive **2,3-BPG depletion**. Consequently, massively transfused patients receive red blood cells with abnormally high oxygen affinity, impairing immediate capillary oxygen release until recipient hepatic and glycolytic enzymes regenerate 2,3-BPG over twelve to twenty-four hours.
steps.say: Stored blood depletes 2,3-BPG, causing tight oxygen binding that takes hours to recover after massive transfusion.

steps.tx: In contrast to normal adult haemoglobin A, human fetal haemoglobin replaces beta-globin with gamma-globin chains containing neutral serine residues at position one hundred forty-three. Lacking the necessary positive charges, fetal haemoglobin cannot effectively bind **intracellular 2,3-BPG**, ensuring higher oxygen affinity than maternal blood across the placenta.
steps.say: Fetal haemoglobin lacks the positive binding site for 2,3-BPG, maintaining high oxygen affinity to extract maternal oxygen.

left.title: Adult Haemoglobin A (α2β2)
points: Beta-chain position 143 has positively charged Histidine
Forms strong electrostatic salt bridges with anionic 2,3-BPG
Moderate baseline oxygen affinity (P50 ~ 26.8 mmHg)
Releases oxygen readily to maternal peripheral tissues

right.title: Fetal Haemoglobin F (α2γ2)
points: Gamma-chain position 143 replaces Histidine with Serine
Neutral serine cannot bind polyanionic 2,3-BPG effectively
Significantly higher oxygen affinity (P50 ~ 19 mmHg)
Extracts oxygen across placental syncytiotrophoblast gradient
